Use them as soon as possible and keep copies of everything. In some situations you have only 30 days after contact to ask for certain information, but the CFPB says it is still worth asking after that. If it is not your debt or you already paid it, documentation helps.

Under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, collectors violate the law when they harass, oppress or abuse you. You can ask them to call at a more convenient time or place. Complaints can be filed with the CFPB. The sample letters are not legal advice.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What should I do when a debt collector contacts me? (last reviewed Aug. 2, 2023)

title: What a Debt Validation Notice Must Include, and the 30-Day Window to Dispute
description: The CFPB lists the information a collector generally must send, and says a written dispute inside 30 days pauses collection until they respond.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: Under the debt collection rule, collectors must give you validation information, generally in a written notice sent as the first communication or within five days of it, by mail or electronically. The CFPB says the notice generally must include: a statement that the communication is from a debt collector; your name and address and the collector’s; the creditor’s name (possibly more than one); the account number, if any; an itemization of the current debt reflecting interest, fees, payments and credits since a given date; the current amount; information for replying if you think the debt is not yours or the amount is wrong; and an end date for a 30-day dispute period.

Once you receive it, you have 30 days to dispute in writing. The CFPB says failing to request verification in writing, or doing it late, can affect your ability to assert your rights under the rule. If you send a written verification request, or ask for information about the original creditor, within the 30 days, the collector must pause collecting the disputed amount until it has adequately responded.
If you think a collector failed to provide the required information, you can submit a complaint with the CFPB.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What information does a debt collector have to give me about a debt they’re trying to collect from me? (last reviewed Jan. 29, 2024)

title: Can Collectors Chase a Debt That Is Several Years Old? What the CFPB Says About Time Limits
description: Debts do not generally expire, but most states limit lawsuits to three to six years. A partial payment may restart the clock.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says a debt does not generally expire or disappear until it is paid, but in many states a statute of limitations limits how long creditors and collectors can use legal action. Most states set limits of three to six years, some longer, and the period can vary by type of debt, your state and the state law named in your agreement. Some debts, such as federal student loans, have no statute of limitations.

When the period starts differs. In some states it begins when a required payment is missed; in others it counts from the most recent payment, even one made during collection. The CFPB warns that a partial payment, or acknowledging you owe an old debt even after the period ends, may restart it.

In most states collectors can still try to collect after the period expires, by letters or calls, if they follow the law. They cannot sue or threaten to sue. A suit on a time-barred debt violates the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, but a court may still enter a judgment if you do not show up and raise the statute of limitations as a defense. The CFPB suggests consulting a lawyer to calculate the period for your debt.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Can debt collectors collect a debt that’s several years old? (last reviewed Dec. 9, 2024)

title: Sued by a Debt Collector? Why Responding Matters, Per the CFPB
description: If you do not respond by the date in the court papers, a default judgment can follow, opening the door to garnishment, liens and frozen accounts.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says anyone sued over an unpaid debt should respond, personally or through a lawyer, by the date in the court papers. Responding does not mean agreeing that you owe the debt; it makes the collector prove the debt is valid, and you may be able to negotiate a settlement.

If you do not respond, the court can enter a default judgment for the amount claimed plus lawful collection costs, interest and attorney fees. Refusing to accept delivery of the lawsuit is unlikely to work, since a court may treat that as ignoring a properly served suit. A judgment is a court order, hard to change afterward, and you may lose the chance to dispute the debt. Depending on your state, the creditor may be able to garnish wages, place a lien on property or move to freeze bank funds.

The agency suggests consulting an attorney, ideally one experienced with the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act; some offer free or reduced-fee services, and legal aid clinics may help if you meet their criteria. Servicemembers can consult their legal assistance office.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What should I do if I’m sued by a debt collector or creditor? (last reviewed Aug. 2, 2023)

title: Can a Debt Collector Garnish Your Wages or Benefits? What the CFPB Says
description: Most creditors need a court judgment first. Banks must protect two months of directly deposited federal benefits.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says most creditors can garnish wages or benefits only after a court issues a judgment saying you owe the debt and allowing garnishment. The order generally covers the judgment amount plus interest, fees and collection costs. Federal and state laws limit how much can be taken and protect a minimum amount in a bank account.

Federal law generally protects some earned wages. Banks must protect two months’ worth of direct-deposited federal benefits before freezing or garnishing money in an account, and you can claim the exemption for up to two months of federal benefits deposited by check. Covered benefits generally include Social Security, Supplemental Security Income, veterans’ benefits, Federal Railroad retirement, unemployment and sickness payments, Civil Service Retirement and Federal Employee Retirement System payments. State exemptions may add protection.

Exceptions: federal and state agencies can sometimes garnish without a court order. Agencies such as the IRS or the Department of Education can take up to 15 percent of Social Security or SSDI benefits, and states can generally garnish wages or bank funds for child support.
The CFPB notes people sometimes learn of a garnishment only when funds are frozen, and says not to ignore a lawsuit. An attorney experienced in consumer law can help you claim exemptions.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Can a debt collector take or garnish my wages or benefits? (last reviewed Aug. 2, 2023)

title: How to Dispute an Error on Your Credit Report, Step by Step (CFPB)
description: Dispute with the credit reporting company first, then with the company that supplied the information. Furnishers generally must respond within 30 days.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says you have the right to dispute credit report errors, and fixing one generally means contacting both the credit reporting company and the company that provided the information. If you suspect identity theft, it points to IdentityTheft.gov.

Start with Experian, Equifax or TransUnion. Explain in writing what is wrong and why, and include supporting documents. A mailed letter should include your name, address and phone number, the report confirmation number if available, each error with its account number, a clear explanation, a request to remove or correct it, a copy of the report section with disputed items marked, and copies, not originals, of supporting documents. You may send it by certified mail with a return receipt. TransUnion takes phone disputes at (800) 916-8800.

The credit reporting company must investigate, forward your dispute and documents to the company that supplied the information, and report results back. It need not investigate disputes it reasonably decides are frivolous or irrelevant, but it must send you a notice explaining why within five business days of that decision.

Then dispute with the furnisher, such as your bank, landlord or card issuer, in writing by certified mail. The CFPB says furnishers generally must investigate and respond within 30 days of receiving the dispute. Keep copies of all letters.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: How do I dispute an error on my credit report? (last reviewed Sept. 2, 2026)

title: Medical Bill Sent to Collections? What the CFPB Says About Surprise-Bill Limits and Credit Reporting
description: Collecting or reporting amounts above what the No Surprises Act permits may violate federal law. Dispute in writing as soon as possible.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says debt collection or credit reporting on medical bills that exceed the amounts permitted by the No Surprises Act, in effect since January 1, 2022 for many surprise medical bills, may violate federal law. Collection agencies and law firms collecting debts can be debt collectors under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, which prohibits false, deceptive or misleading statements about the character, amount or legal status of a debt. A collector cannot misrepresent that you must pay a charge exceeding what the Act permits.

If you believe a collector is trying to collect more than the No Surprises Act allows, the CFPB says to dispute in writing as soon as possible, which protects your FDCPA rights and puts the collector on notice. The Fair Credit Reporting Act also sets accuracy requirements for credit bureaus and the collectors that report to them.

Help: submit a CFPB complaint at (855) 411-2372 if a collector contacts you about a surprise medical bill or such charges appear as negative items on your credit report; call the CMS No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET, seven days a week; speak with a lawyer or free legal services; servicemembers can use legal assistance offices; and file with your state attorney general, since states may add protections.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What should I know about debt collection and credit reporting if my medical bill was sent to collections? (last reviewed July 25, 2025)

title: What Happens If Your Car Is Repossessed? Your Rights, Per the CFPB
description: Notice rules vary by state. Lenders may not “breach the peace,” and a repossession can stay on your credit reports for up to seven years.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says that in many states a lender can repossess a vehicle without warning or a court order after a missed payment, while other states require notice first. Active-duty servicemembers are protected by the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which bars repossession without a court order for auto loans entered before military service. Auto loan servicers must ensure every repossession is lawful; if you think it was an error, contact the lender or servicer right away, then complain or pursue court action if unresolved.

Under some state laws a lender cannot repossess if it requires “breaching the peace,” which generally means threatening or using physical force, removing a vehicle from a closed garage without permission, or continuing after you refuse. You may contact law enforcement, and it may give you a claim for damages or a defense that lowers what you owe after sale.

Belongings in the car: contact the lender right away to retrieve them and document what was inside. The CFPB found in an enforcement action that withholding property unless consumers paid an upfront fee was an unfair practice. A repossession can stay on your credit reports up to seven years, and can raise insurance rates. If it was an error, dispute it with the credit bureaus.

Some states let you pay overdue amounts and repossession costs to get the vehicle back, called curing or reinstating the loan. In any case you have the right to be notified before the vehicle is sold or kept as compensation, giving you the chance to buy it back.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What happens if my car is repossessed?

title: Charged an Overdraft Fee? Opt-In Rules for Debit Cards, and Where They Do Not Apply
description: Banks cannot charge overdraft fees on one-time debit and ATM transactions unless you opted in, but checks and recurring payments are different.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says banks cannot charge an overdraft fee on one-time debit card transactions and ATM withdrawals unless you opt in to overdraft protection. They may charge overdraft fees on checks and recurring electronic payments even if you did not opt in.

Declining overdraft protection means no fee on debit and ATM transactions, but overdrawing with a check or recurring electronic payment can still cost a fee. Some banks let you opt out of those overdrafts, but you may then face a non-sufficient funds fee, often the same amount as an overdraft fee, and declined payments can trigger a returned-item fee from the merchant.

If you are enrolled, you can change your mind at any time by telling your bank or credit union. If you do not believe you authorized debit overdraft protection and were charged a debit overdraft fee, you can file a complaint with the CFPB.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What can I do if my bank charged me a fee for overdrawing my account? (page last modified Jan. 2, 2025)

title: Credit Counseling vs. Debt Settlement vs. Credit Repair: The CFPB’s Differences
description: Counselors are usually nonprofits. Settlement and repair companies are typically for-profit and charge for steps you can take yourself for free.
author: Kseniya Dzigava
body: The CFPB says credit counseling organizations are usually nonprofits that advise and educate you on money and debts, while debt settlement companies, debt consolidation lenders and credit repair companies are typically for-profit businesses that charge for actions you can often take yourself for free.

Credit counselors usually offer free educational materials and workshops, with an initial session of about an hour. They can set up a debt management plan: you make one monthly payment to the organization, which pays your creditors. They cannot erase debts and may charge fees. They work to lower your monthly payment, such as by lengthening terms or lowering interest rates, rather than reducing what you owe. They help with budgets, get creditors to agree not to pursue collection or charge late fees during the plan, and never advise you to stop paying your debts.

Debt settlement companies offer to resolve debts for a fee, usually by lump-sum payments you save up first. Money in a settlement account still belongs to you, must be held by an independent third party under your control, and you may withdraw it any time without penalty. The CFPB cautions that many lenders do not negotiate with settlement companies, that they usually cannot get better terms than you could yourself, and that they cannot guarantee savings, timing or erasing all debts. They often advise you to stop paying creditors, even though fees and interest keep adding up, your credit suffers and collection efforts can increase.

sources.label: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: What is the difference between credit counseling and debt settlement, debt consolidation, or credit repair? (last reviewed May 15, 2024)
